We have mass spec: m/z 127.0997 (intensity 100) likely molecular ion. That mass corresponds to formula? Let's compute: C8H15? mass of C8H15? C8=96, H15=15.117, total 111.117. Not 127.1. C9H11? C9=108, H11=11.086=119.086. C7H11O? C7=84, H11=11.086, O=15.995 =111.081. Need 127.0997. Could be C8H15O? 96+15.117+15.995=127.112. That's close. So formula likely C8H15O (M+? maybe radical cation). So molecular formula C8H16O? Actually neutral C8H16O mass = 128.125? Let's compute: C8H16O = 96 + 16.125 + 15.995 = 128.12. The observed m/z 127.0997 could be M+? maybe M+H? Actually ESI positive mode often gives [M+H]+. If M = 126.099? Let's compute C8H14O: 96 + 14.109 + 15.995 = 126.104. + H = 127.112. So observed 127.0997 matches C8H15O+ (M+H). So neutral formula C8H14O. So DBE = (2C+2 - H)/2 = (16+2-14)/2 = (4)/2=2. So two degrees unsaturation. Could be carbonyl (1) + ring (1) or double bond (2). NMR: proton NMR shows three singlets: 1.78 (s, 3H), 1.92 (s, 6H), 2.65 (s, 3H). Total integration 12 H. But formula has 14 H. Wait integration maybe not exact? 3+6+3 =12. Missing 2 H maybe overlapping? Could be a CH2 not observed? But all singlets suggests no coupling, maybe methyl groups attached to carbonyl or quaternary carbon. 2.65 ppm is relatively downfield for methyl next to carbonyl (acetyl methyl ~2.1). 2.65 could be methyl attached to carbonyl and also to something else like alpha to carbonyl? Actually acetyl methyl appears ~2.1. 2.65 maybe methyl attached to carbonyl and also to aromatic? Not.

But we have 3 singlets: 6H suggests two equivalent methyls (maybe isopropyl? but that would be doublet). So two identical methyl groups attached to same carbon (tert-butyl). So t-butyl gives 9H singlet ~1.4. Here we have 6H at 1.92, maybe two methyls attached to same carbon (isopropyl? but that gives doublet). Could be gem-dimethyl attached to carbonyl (acetone). For example, pinacolone (tert-butyl methyl ketone) has t-Bu (9H) and acetyl methyl (3H). Not match.

Our integration 6H suggests two equivalent methyls maybe on a carbon adjacent to carbonyl? Eg. acetone (CH3)2C=O gives 6H singlet at ~2.1. That's 6H singlet. Here we have 6H at 1.92, plausible. Then another 3H singlet at 1.78 maybe another methyl attached to something else (maybe attached to carbonyl as well). And 3H singlet at 2.65 maybe methyl attached to carbonyl (acetyl). So total 12H, but formula C8H14O has 14 H. So missing 2 H maybe part of CH2 group not observed due to overlapping? But we have only singlets, maybe CH2 attached to carbonyl (alpha) appears as multiplet ~2.3-2.5, not singlet. Could be CH2 attached to O (ether) appears ~3.5.

Maybe the sample is an ester: e.g., methyl isobutyrate? That has CH3COOCH3: protons: OCH3 ~3.7 (singlet 3H), CH3CO ~2.1 (singlet 3H), and isobutyl CH3 groups? Actually isobutyl group has CH2CH(CH3)2 giving multiplets.

Our data: three singlets only, suggests molecule with only methyl groups and no other protons. That would be something like C8H14O with only methyls and maybe a quaternary carbon and carbonyl. Example: 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanone? Let's think: 2,2-dimethylpropanal? That's C5H10O. Not.

Consider 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanone (pinacolone) formula C6H12O? Actually pinacolone is (CH3)3C-CO-CH3: C6? Wait t-Bu (C4) + CO + CH3 = C6? Actually t-Bu is C4H9, plus carbonyl carbon = C5, plus methyl = C6. So C6H12O. Not.

Our formula C8H14O could be a cyclic ketone with two methyl groups? Example: 3,3-dimethylcyclohexanone? That would have C8? Cyclohexanone C6H10O, plus two methyls = C8H14O. Yes cyclohexanone (C6H10O) plus two methyls at same carbon (C8H14O). That would have 6-member ring with carbonyl, and gem-dimethyl at position 3 maybe. Protons: gem-dimethyl (6H) singlet ~1.2-1.5. The other methyl? Actually gem-dimethyl gives 6H. Additional methyl? Wait we have only two methyl groups (6H) plus maybe other methyls? But we have 3 singlets: 6H (gem-dimethyl), 3H (maybe methyl attached to carbonyl? but carbonyl already part of ring). In cyclohexanone, there is no methyl attached to carbonyl. So maybe it's a methyl ketone attached to cyclopentane? Eg. 3-methylcyclohexanone? That would have one methyl (3H) and ring protons.

But we have only methyl signals, no ring CH. So maybe the molecule is a symmetric di-ketone with only methyls? Eg. 2,5-hexanedione? That has CH3-CO-CH2-CH2-CO-CH3: would have CH2 signals.

Thus maybe the sample is an ester with only methyl groups: e.g., dimethyl adipate? That has CH3O-CO-(CH2)4-CO-OCH3, includes CH2.

Thus maybe the sample is a tertiary butyl acetate? t-BuOCOCH3: formula C6H12O2. Not.

Our mass suggests C8H14O, DBE=2. Could be a cyclic ether (one DBE ring) plus carbonyl (another DBE). So maybe a lactone: e.g., gamma-butyrolactone with two methyl substituents? Example: 3,3-dimethyl-2-oxetanone? Not.

Consider methyl cyclopentanone with gem-dimethyl? Actually cyclopentanone C5H8O, plus two methyls = C7H12O. Not.

Maybe it's a cyclic ester (lactone) with two methyl groups: e.g., 3,3-dimethyl-2-oxetanone (four-member lactone) formula C5H8O2? Not.

Let's compute formula for 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanone? Already C6.

We need C8H14O, DBE=2. Could be a cyclohexenone (one double bond + carbonyl) with methyl substituents. Cyclohexenone (C6H8O) DBE=2. Add two methyls gives C8H12O? Actually add two CH3 adds C2H6 => C8H14O. Yes cyclohexenone (C6H8O) plus two methyl groups (C2H6) gives C8H14O. So maybe 2-methyl-3-methylcyclohex-2-enone? But then there would be olefinic protons.

But NMR shows only singlets, no olefinic protons. So maybe the double bond is conjugated but fully substituted (no H). Example: 2,5-dimethyl-2,5-dihydro-1,3-dioxin? Not.

Consider a cyclic ketone with a double bond but fully substituted: e.g., 3,3-dimethylcyclohex-2-en-1-one? That would have a carbonyl at position 1, double bond between 2-3, but 3 is gem-dimethyl, so double bond carbon 2 has no H, carbon 3 has no H (substituted). So no olefinic H. The ring also has other CH2s that would show multiplets. But we only see singlets.

Thus maybe the molecule is a highly symmetric with only methyl groups and no other protons: e.g., 2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-4-pentanone? Not.

Let's think of a molecule with only methyl groups and maybe a carbonyl, but no CH. That would be a quaternary carbon attached to carbonyl and methyls, plus maybe another carbonyl? Example: diacetyl (2,3-butanedione) C4H6O2, has CH3 groups (2*3=6 H) and no other H. That's 2 CH3 singlets? Actually both CH3 are equivalent? They are not equivalent due to symmetry? They appear as singlet 2.2 ppm (6H). Our data has three singlets, so maybe a molecule with three distinct methyl groups attached to carbonyl(s) and maybe an ether.

Consider acetylacetone (pentane-2,4-dione) C5H8O2, has CH3 groups (2*3=6) and a CH (1H) at central carbon, not.

Our data: 6H singlet at 1.92 (likely gem-dimethyl attached to carbonyl). 3H singlet at 1.78 (maybe methyl attached to carbonyl but more shielded). 3H singlet at 2.65 (more deshielded, maybe methyl attached to carbonyl directly). Could be a tert-butyl acetate? t-BuOCOCH3: has t-Bu (9H) and acetyl methyl (3H). Not match.

Maybe it's methyl isobutyrate? CH3CH(CH3)COOCH3: protons: OCH3 (3H singlet ~3.7), CH3 attached to carbonyl (3H singlet ~2.1), CH3 attached to CH (doublet). Not.

Our data lacks OCH3 at ~3.7, so not ester.

Could be a ketone with two gem-dimethyl groups: e.g., pinacolone (tert-butyl methyl ketone) C6H12O, has 9H singlet (t-Bu) and 3H singlet (acetyl). Not.

Our formula C8H14O suggests maybe a ketone with two gem-dimethyl groups: e.g., 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanone? That's C6. Need C8, so maybe 3,3-dimethyl-2-pentanone? That is (CH3)2C-CO-CH2-CH3? That has CH2 and CH3 not singlet.

Maybe it's a cyclic ketone with gem-dimethyl and a methyl attached to carbonyl (acetyl). Example: 3,3-dimethylcyclohexanone with an extra acetyl? Not.

Let's compute possible structure: C8H14O could be an isobutyl methyl ketone? CH3-CO-CH2-CH(CH3)2: that's 2-methyl-2-butanone? Actually 2-methyl-2-butanone (pinacolone) is C6. 3-methyl-2-butanone is C5? Hmm.

Better approach: Use search by SMILES? Could try to search NMRShift DB for candidate matching mass 127.099 (M+H). But we can also generate isomers list for C8H14O and test NMR predictions. Use obtain_isomers_from_molecular_formula gave many candidates, but we can test each with proton_nmr_spectra to see if matches pattern. But that's many calls; we should be selective.

We need a molecule with only methyl protons (singlets). So candidate must have no CH, CH2, aromatic etc. Only CH3 groups attached to quaternary carbons or heteroatoms. So the structure must be a tertiary carbon attached to three methyls (tert-butyl) and carbonyl maybe. That gives 9H singlet. But we have 6H and two 3H singlets, total 12H. So maybe two gem-dimethyl groups (6H each) but they are not equivalent (different chemical shifts). That gives 12H. Plus maybe a carbonyl methyl (3H) gives 15H, too many. But we have 12H total observed, maybe missing 2H due to overlapping with solvent? Could be CH2 not observed.

But integration may be approximate. Could be 6H gem-dimethyl, 3H methyl attached to carbonyl, and 3H methyl attached to oxygen (OCH3) which appears ~3.7 not 2.65. So not.

The 2.65 ppm is relatively downfield for methyl next to carbonyl and also attached to electronegative group like O? Actually OCH3 ~3.3-3.8. So 2.65 maybe alpha to carbonyl (CH3-CO-). So that's acetyl methyl.

Thus maybe molecule is isobutyl acetate? OCH3 not present.

Let's compute mass of acetylacetone (C5H8O2) not.

Maybe the molecule is 2,2-dimethyl-3-oxobutanoic acid? Not.

Given limited time, maybe the correct SMILES is "CC(C)C(=O)C(C)C". Let's compute formula: CC(C)C(=O)C(C)C = 2,4-dimethyl-2-pentanone? Actually that's C7? Count: C: 7? Let's count: CC(C)C(=O)C(C)C: chain: C C (C) C(=O) C(C) C. That's 7 carbons? Let's count: first C (CH3), second C (CH with branch), branch (C) methyl, carbonyl carbon, then C with branch methyl, then terminal C. total 7? Actually maybe C8. Let's count: atoms: CH3- (C1), CH (C2) attached to CH3 (C3) and carbonyl C4, then carbonyl carbon (C4), then CH (C5) attached to CH3 (C6) and CH3 (C7). That's 7 carbons. So formula C7H14O? Not.

Our mass suggests C8. Let's try "CC(C)C(=O)CC(C)C". That's 3,5-dimethyl-2-hexanone? Count C: 8. Formula C8H16O? Actually H count: each CH3 3, CH (attached to two CH3 and carbonyl) is CH, etc. Might be C8H16O. Not.

But neutral formula should be C8H14O. So need two degrees unsaturation: carbonyl (1) and maybe a double bond (C=C) or ring. If we have a carbonyl and a double bond fully substituted, could have only methyls. Example: 2,4-dimethyl-3-penten-2-one? That has CH3-CO-CH= C(CH3)-CH3? That has CH3 at carbonyl (3H), two methyls on double bond (6H), and maybe another methyl? Actually formula maybe C7? Not.

Let's try a conjugated diene carbonyl with no H on double bond: e.g., 3,3-dimethyl-2-buten-1-one? That's isopropenyl methyl ketone? Not.

Better: Use tool search_by_smiles to find similar to known patterns? Could try to search for C8H14O with only methyl groups. Let's try to generate candidate SMILES: "CC(C)(C)C(=O)C(C)(C)C" that's pivalone? That's C8? Actually that's tert-butyl acetone? That would be (CH3)3C-CO-C(CH3)3, which is C8? Wait each t-Bu is C4, two t-Bu gives C8, plus carbonyl carbon is already counted? Actually each t-Bu includes carbonyl carbon? The carbonyl carbon is central, attached to two t-Bu groups: (CH3)3C-CO-C(CH3)3 is C8? Count: each t-Bu has 4 carbons, two t-Bu =8, plus carbonyl carbon is one of them? Actually carbonyl carbon is part of the central carbon? The structure is (CH3)3C-CO- C(CH3)3, carbonyl carbon is separate, so total C = 4+4+1 =9. So not.

But maybe the molecule is "CC(C)C(=O)C(C)(C)C"? That's 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanone? Count: left side CH3-CH(CH3)-CO- C(CH3)2? That's C7? Let's compute: left side: CH3 (C1), CH (C2), branch CH3 (C3), carbonyl C4, right side carbon attached to two CH3 (C5 central, C6, C7). That's 7. Not.

We need C8. Could be "CC(C)C(=O)C(C)(C)C" actually has extra CH3? Wait right side central carbon is quaternary with two CH3 and maybe one CH3? Actually C(C)(C)C means carbon attached to three CH3 groups (tert-butyl). So carbonyl attached to tert-butyl on one side and isopropyl on other? That would be C9.

Let's try to use obtain_isomers list and filter for those with only methyl groups. Look at list: e.g., 'CC(C)[C@@H]1CC[C@H]2[C@@H]1O2' has ring and O. Not.

'C/C=C\\C[C@@H](C)C(=O)C' has double bond and carbonyl, also CH2.

'CCCC(C=CC=C)O' has aromatic.

'C/C=C/CCCC1CO1' has ring.

'CC1(C2C1C(CC2)O)C' maybe bicyclic with OH.

'CCO/C=C/C/C=C/C' has OCH2.

'CCC1CC(=CO1)CC' has carbonyl in ring.

'CCC(C=O)C(=C)CC' has double bond.

'CC1(C2C1CCC2)CO' maybe.

We need only methyls and carbonyl, no other protons. None of these.

Maybe the sample is a simple ketone: 2,2-dimethyl-3-butanone? Actually 2,2-dimethyl-3-butanone (pinacolone) is C6.

But C8H14O could be 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanone? That's C6.

Maybe it's 2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-4-pentanone? That's C9.

Given difficulty, maybe the correct SMILES is "CC(C)C(=O)C(C)C". Let's compute formula: C7? Let's compute using tool.
